title: King's Indian: critical sidelines and move-order tricks
question: When White avoids the main line with Sämisch, Four Pawns, Averbakh, a fianchetto or the Exchange, what does each choice buy and cost, and how does Black answer?
outcomes: Names the five main King's Indian sidelines and says what each buys and what it costs
Chooses Black's strike against Sämisch and Four Pawns and says why a quiet move is worse
Counts the guards of e4 before capturing in the Averbakh and avoids the knight capture that loses material
Recognises when two move orders reach one position and plays the position, not the move string
Answers the knight jump to d5 in the Exchange line and reads game counts as results with a sample size

steps.chapter: Five questions put to one player

steps.prompt: Guess before you read on. Name one way White could avoid the main fight, and one thing that choice gives up.

steps.text: **What you will be able to do.** Most King's Indian games leave the main line early. Five sidelines each put a different question to Black: a solid centre (Sämisch), extra space (Four Pawns), pressure on f6 (Averbakh), a quiet fianchetto, and a queen trade (Exchange). For each you will say **what White buys, what it costs, and Black's best reply**, and you will see how two move orders can reach one position.

**The Sämisch pawn move (f3).** The pawn on f3 gives e4 a second guard, so a black knight cannot simply win it, and it prepares Be3, Qd2 and long castling. The price [I]: the f3 square is no longer free for the knight, and the pawn has left the g1-a7 diagonal open. The move appears 654 times in 5,565 master games after 4...d6 [V]. Next, count the guards of e4.

steps.text: **[H] Why do masters still play ...e5?** The engine prefers ...c5 by about 0.3 pawn, but masters chose ...e5 almost as often. Two conjectures, both untested here: the locked structure gives Black a clear plan (the f-pawn storm), or players simply know that structure better. Which would you test first, and how? Write a line.

steps.text: **The Four Pawns Attack (f4).** White plays c4, d4, e4 and f4: the most space any white set-up takes, with the threat of e5 hitting the knight. The price [I]: four pawns far from home need guarding and the king has few shields near the centre. It is rare: 89 of 5,565 master games after 4...d6 [V]. Black's recipe: strike the centre before White's pieces are ready.

steps.text: **The condition.** Moves that do not prepare an answer to the e5 push (...Nbd7, ...e6, ...a5) score about 0.6 to 0.8 pawn worse here. A developing move that pins or pre-empts (...Bg4, ...Na6) can still be fine. The strike needs a target (d4 or e4) and a way to meet the advance. Always ask: *what does the next pawn push attack, and what answers it?*

steps.text: **The Averbakh set-up (Be2, then Bg5).** The bishop on g5 attacks the knight on f6 and waits: once Black's e-pawn moves, the bishop pins the knight against the queen. White develops the bishop to e2 first and keeps a knight or pawn move in reserve. After 5.Be2 O-O, 254 of 1,455 master games played the bishop move 6.Bg5 [V]. Black has several good answers, but one natural capture is a trap.

steps.title: Is the capture on e4 safe?
steps.prompt: Three positions, one question: Black's knight takes on e4. Predict each, then check. If you want an example first, step through the count diagram again.

steps.text: **Count before you capture.** Count the guards on both sides, then compare what each capture gives and gets, in order. Here one attacker meets one guard: ...Nxe4 Nxe4 gives a knight (about three pawns) for a pawn. Habit: before ...Nxe4, name every guard, then add up what you give and get.

**Two quiet roads.** In the *Fianchetto* White plays g3 and puts the bishop on g2, keeping the centre flexible. In the *Exchange* line White trades pawns and then queens. Both are slow, so the question is who has the better pawn break. They also show **transpositions**: different move orders that reach the same position, so learn positions, not move strings. First, the Fianchetto reached in two ways.

steps.text: **The Exchange line.** White trades pawns on d6/e5 and offers the queens. It is solid and rarely sharp: after the queens leave, the fight is about the open d-file and the weak c7 pawn. The danger for Black is the white knight landing on d5. Step through the line, then find Black's answer to the knight jump.

steps.text: **Reading the numbers.** The Exchange line, once the queens are off, appeared in 102 master games: White won 18, 71 were drawn (70%), Black won 13 [V]. In the position just before the pawn trade (2499 games) 41% were drawn [V]. [H] The queen trade removes most of White's winning attempts, so the line suits a player who wants a draw with White. Games, not verdicts: we have not tested why.

steps.prompt: Would you choose the Exchange line as White, or play against it as Black? Give one reason from the numbers or the structure, and one thing you would still want to check.

steps.text: **Choosing your answer.** Ask three questions of any sideline. *What does it buy?* (centre, space, a pin, a quiet game.) *What does it cost?* (a weakness, a tempo.) *Which of my pawn breaks hits that cost first?* Against Sämisch and Four Pawns: strike the centre early. Against Averbakh: count e4 before you capture. Against the quiet lines: keep your pieces and find the break.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine a club player who meets a sideline they do not know. In your own words write: the idea (what White buys and pays), when Black's recipe works, one example a beginner can set up on a board, and one warning.

steps.text: **Recap and self-check.** Sämisch: f3 holds e4, so strike the centre. Four Pawns: space is a target, strike before e5. Averbakh: count e4 before capturing. Fianchetto: slow, and move orders transpose. Exchange: watch the knight jump to d5.
